items.actClause: AN ACT to amend the general business law, in relation to providing for enhanced consumer protection measures and enforcement of the do-not-call registry
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER:A8839

TITLE OF BILL:

An act to amend the general business law, in relation to providing for
enhanced consumer protection measures and enforcement of the do-not-call
registry

PURPOSE OR GENERAL IDEA OF BILL:

This purpose of this bill is to enhance the Consumer Protection Board's
ability to protect consumers from unsolicited telemarketing sales calls
and enforce the Do-Not-Call law.

SUMMARY OF SPECIFIC PROVISIONS:

This bill would enhance the Consumer Protection Board's (CPB) ability to
protect consumers from unsolicited telemarketing sales calls and enforce
the Do-Not-Call law by limiting the time of the day that a telemarketer
may call a residence to the period from 8:00 a.m. to 9:00 p.m. and
requiring telemarketers to provide consumers with the identity of the
telemarketer and seller, the purpose of the call, the identity and cost
of the goods or services being offered, and the terms and conditions
related to any offers that include a negative option feature. The bill
would also clarify that prerecorded telephone messages and any message
delivered to a consumer's voicemail or answering machine are included
within the existing definition of "telemarketing sales call." These
changes would conform New York law to the Federal Trade Commission's
Telemarketing Sales Rule. Lastly, the bill would authorize the CPB to
issue subpoenas during the investigatory phase of its telemarketing
enforcement proceedings.

JUSTIFICATION:

Since the State's Do-Not-Call (DNC) law became effective in April 2001,
it has become one of the most important consumer laws enacted in New
York State. DNC is the most common subject of complaint received by the
CPB's Consumer Assistance Unit. In the first two quarters of 2008, the
total number of DNC related complaints or inquiries totaled 52,425.
However, notwithstanding its popularity, the statute needs to be revised
to reflect new telemarketing practices and trends.

To save time and resources, many companies are turning to automatic
prerecorded calling as opposed to live person-to-person calling. By
further defining "telemarketing sales call" in the DNC statute to
include any outbound telephone calling technology that delivers pre-re-
corded unsolicited telemarketing sales call message either to a customer
or to their voicemail or answering machine service, the CPB seeks to
create more comprehensive protections for consumers. These amendments
are consistent with current federal TCPA protections and bring the State
law into parity with the federal law in this regard.

This bill clarifies that prerecorded unsolicited telemarketing sales
calls are subject to the same enforcement provisions as "live" calls, as
they are just as onerous and burdensome to New Yorkers who do not want
to receive unsolicited calls. Further, it is important to limit the time
of day that a telemarketer may call a consumer. The CPB enforcement
staff has received numerous complaints relating to disruptive late night
and early morning telemarketing calls.  While the federal law contains
this prohibition, the current State law does not. This bill would
restrict telemarketing calls to between the hours of 8 a.m. and 9 p.m.

In addition, the bill requires a telemarketer to provide consumers with
his or her name, the entity on whose behalf the call is made, the
purpose of the call, and the identity and cost of the goods or services
being offered. Such information would allow consumers to determine the
nature of the call and make informed choices, and aid enforcement by the
CPB.

Many consumers have been frustrated by trial offers which invite their
business for what seems to the consumer to be for a limited time, only
for the consumer to realize they have signed onto a longer term commit-
ment. This bill requires telemarketers and sellers to communicate all of
the material terms and conditions of an offer when such offer contains a
"negative option" feature, wherein the consumer is required to take
affirmative steps to reject further provision of goods and services.
This provision is consistent with the TSR and creates parity between
State and federal law.

Finally, the bill would grant CPB the power to subpoena documents and
records related to possible violations of this provision. This would
greatly aid in enforcement of this provision, and in ensuring that
violators receive appropriate sanction.

PRIOR LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

New bill.

FISCAL IMPLICATIONS FOR STATE AND LOCAL GOVERNMENTS

None.

EFFECTIVE DATE:

One-hundred eightieth day.

A.memo:
BILL NUMBER:A8839A

TITLE OF BILL:  An act to amend the general business law, in relation to
providing for enhanced consumer protection measures and enforcement of
the do-not-call registry

Purpose:  This bill amends the do-not-call law to create more comprehen-
sive protections from unsolicited telemarketing sales calls for consum-
ers.  The bill expressly prohibits pre-recorded telemarketing sales
calls; restricts telemarketer calling times; requires telemarketers to
disclose all terms and conditions related to offers containing negative
option features; and provides the Consumer Protection Board (CPB) with
subpoena power to investigate violations.

Summary of Provisions:  Section 1 of the bill amends General Business
Law (GBL) § 399-z to do the following:

* define the term "negative option feature."

* include within the definition of "telemarketing sales call" any
outbound telephone calling technology that delivers a prerecorded unso-
licited telemarketing message to a customer or to his or her voicemail
or answering machine service.

* limit the time of day that a telemarketer may call and requires a
telemarketer to provide consumers with its name, the purpose of the
call, and the identity and cost of the goods or services being offered,
and the terms and conditions related to any offers that include a nega-
tive option.

* provide the CPB with subpoena power during the investigatory phase of
its enforcement proceedings.

* clarify the elements to be established for an alleged violator to
assert a defense under this section.

* renumber various provisions in the interest of consistency with the
amended law.

Section 2 of the bill provides that it would take effect one hundred and
twenty days after it becomes law.

Existing Law:  Currently, GBL § 399-z bars any telemarketer or seller
from making any unsolicited telemarketing sales call to any customer
when that customer's telephone number has been on the national "do-not-
call" registry.

The federal Telemarketing Sales Rule (TSR) requires telemarketers to
call only between 8:00 am. and 9:00 p.m. local time and requires them to
disclose truthfully, promptly, and clearly and conspicuously, the (1)
identity of the seller/telemarketer; ( 2) that the purpose of the call

is to sell goods or services; and (3) the nature of the goods and
services. (16 CFR § 310.4)

The TSR, 16 CFR Part 310 et seq. prohibits certain telemarketing sales
practices. Specifically, the TSR requires telemarketers to disclose all
material terms and conditions of any offer that contains a negative
option feature.

The federal Telephone Consumer Protection Act of 1991 (TCPA), among
other provisions, restricts the use of automatic dialing systems and
prerecorded or artificial messages. One of its implementing rules, 47
CFR § 64.200, prohibits any telemarketer from using an artificial or
prerecorded voice to deliver a message without the prior express consent
of the called party.

Statement in Support:  Since the State's Do-Not Call (DNC) law became
effective in April 2001, it has become one of the most important consum-
er laws enacted in New York State. DNC is the most common subject of
complaint received by the CPB's Consumer Assistance Unit. In the first
two quarters of 2008, the total number of DNC related complaints or
inquiries totaled 52,425. However, notwithstanding its popularity, the

In addition, the bill requires a telemarketer to provide consumers with

Budget Implications: None.

Effective Date:  This act takes effect on the one hundred twentieth day
after it shall have become law.

summary: Provides for enhanced consumer protection measures and enforcement of the do-not-call registry; limits telemarketing to 8 am to 9 pm local time unless given express permission by the consumer to contact at a different time.
